title: A glimpse of the distant past
caption: The lensing galaxy cluster Abell S1063, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Abell S1063 · constellation Grus · about 4 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, H. Atek, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb)Acknowledgement: R. Endsley

recognition.text: Ranked #41 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: An enormous bright-white elliptical galaxy sits at the heart of this Webb view, surrounded by other ellipticals and by short, curved, glowing red lines. The white galaxies make up the cluster Abell S1063, about 4.5 billion light-years away in Grus, the Crane. The red arcs are the main target, faint galaxies from the universe's distant past.

The cluster acts as a strong gravitational lens. Its mass is so great that light from galaxies lined up behind it bends around it, and like a glass lens it focuses that light, making the background galaxies brighter and larger, though distorted. Hubble's Frontier Fields programme had already used it as a magnifying glass on the early universe.

Webb pushes further back. This is a deep field, a long exposure of one patch of sky, built from 9 separate near-infrared snapshots adding up to around 120 hours. With the lens's help, it is Webb's deepest look at any single target so far.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.31 x 2.21 arcminutes) and distance (4 billion light years), the frame spans roughly 2.7 million × 2.6 million light-years. Its light set out about 4,000 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed through nine near-infrared filters, mapped from purple and blue for the shortest wavelengths through green, yellow and orange to red for the longest.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and around 120 hours of observing collect far more light than any eye could.

explore: The data come from the GLIMPSE programme, which aims to probe Cosmic Dawn, the era of the first galaxies. The team has already found candidate galaxies from only 200 million years after the Big Bang, along with hints of the elusive first population of stars. A couple of foreground stars look big and bright, with long spikes.
alt: A huge bright-white elliptical galaxy at the centre of a cluster of ellipticals, ringed by short curved red arcs, with a couple of bright spiked foreground stars.
